\chapter{Awake, Asleep, Strong, Weak}
\label{ch:despierto-y-sano}
\hlchaptermodality{327}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can report on my body with despierto, dormido, fuerte, debil and sano, and say why a vowel breaks in duermo but not in dormido.}

Complete ES-C327-sano: say estoy despierto and estoy dormido, put fuerte against debil, and close with sano y salvo.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[despierto]{despierto — the e that breaks, and where it breaks}

\label{lesson:ES-C327-despierto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{free}, then \emph{I am ready}. (\emph{Libre}; \emph{estoy listo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item e $\to$ ie and o $\to$ ue — the break this word walks.
  \item regular — a distant relative, further down.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{des-PYER-to}, the weight on the middle beat. The \emph{ie} is one glide, not two vowels, and the \emph{r} is a single flick. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{despierto} — \textquotedblleft{}awake.\textquotedblright{}

Start with the verb behind it, \textbf{despertar}, \emph{to wake}. Latin \textbf{expergīscī} meant \emph{to wake up}, and it is built from \emph{ex-}, \emph{out of}, plus \textbf{pergere}, \emph{to press onward} — waking as setting out again. \emph{Pergere} is itself \emph{per-} plus \textbf{regere}, \emph{to steer}, and that one is loud in English: to \textbf{direct}, to \textbf{correct}, a \textbf{region}, a \textbf{regent}, a \textbf{rule}, and the \emph{regula} behind \emph{regular}.

Now the sound. The infinitive is \emph{despertar}, with an \emph{e}. The form you say about yourself is \emph{despierto}, with an \emph{ie}. This is the break you were shown long ago, and it obeys one condition: the \emph{e} splits into \emph{ie} only where the stress falls on it. In \emph{despertar} the weight is on the last beat, so the \emph{e} stays whole. In \emph{despierto} the weight moves onto the stem, and the vowel cracks.

Then the useful accident. \textbf{Despierto} is both \emph{I wake up} and the adjective \emph{awake} — the same six letters. \emph{Estoy despierto} is \emph{I am awake}, and the \emph{-o} switches for a woman: \textbf{despierta}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five reports from the body rather than the mind.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{despierto}
  \item \emph{estoy despierto}
  \item \emph{despertar — despierto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \emph{despertar} keep its \emph{e} while \emph{despierto} breaks it? (The break happens only where the stress lands.) And what did \emph{expergīscī} picture waking as? (Setting out again.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dormido]{dormido — a verb you have and an ending you have}

\label{lesson:ES-C327-dormido}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I am ready}, then \emph{I am awake}. (\emph{Estoy listo}; \emph{estoy despierto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item dormir — the verb this is built from.
  \item hablado / comido / vivido — the ending being put on it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dor-MEE-do}, the weight on the middle beat. The \emph{r} is one flick, and the \emph{d} between vowels softens toward the \emph{th} of \emph{this}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dormido} — \textquotedblleft{}asleep.\textquotedblright{}

Nothing is new here. You have the verb \textbf{dormir} and you have the \emph{-ido} ending, so \emph{dormir} plus \emph{-ido} gives \textbf{dormido}, and a participle used as an adjective is \emph{asleep}: \textbf{estoy dormido}.

Latin \textbf{dormīre} stayed close to the surface in English, always in places where sleep is the point. A \textbf{dormitory} is a sleeping-room. A \textbf{dormant} seed is sleeping. A \textbf{dormer} window began as the window of a sleeping-room in the roof. And a \textbf{dormouse} is not a door-mouse — the first half is \emph{dormīre} arriving through French, the mouse that sleeps all winter.

Here is the sound point, and it closes the one from last time. \emph{Dormir} breaks its \emph{o} into \emph{ue} when you say \emph{duermo} — but \emph{dormido} does not break at all. Same rule, applied honestly: the vowel cracks only under stress. In \emph{duermo} the weight is on the stem; in \emph{dormido} it has moved onto the \emph{-i-}, so the \emph{o} stays whole. Awake and asleep both turn out to be lessons about where the stress is standing.

The \emph{-o} switches: \textbf{dormida}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The pair — awake and asleep — and one sound rule proved twice in a row.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dormido}
  \item \emph{estoy dormido}
  \item \emph{despierto — dormido}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \emph{duermo} break its \emph{o} while \emph{dormido} does not? (The break needs the stress, and in \emph{dormido} the stress has moved.) And what is sleeping inside the English \emph{dormouse}? (\emph{Dormīre}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fuerte]{fuerte — the adjective under a noun you already carry}

\label{lesson:ES-C327-fuerte}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I am awake}, then \emph{asleep}. (\emph{Estoy despierto}; \emph{dormido}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la fuerza — the noun; this is the adjective it was built from.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FWER-te}, two beats, the weight on the first. The \emph{ue} is one glide starting with a \emph{w}, and the \emph{r} is a single flick. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{fuerte} — \textquotedblleft{}strong.\textquotedblright{} And, said about a sound, \textquotedblleft{}loud.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{fortis} meant \emph{strong}, and Spanish already handed you the noun: \emph{la fuerza}, from \emph{fortia}, is the strength. This is the adjective standing behind it, and it walked the same road — the stressed \emph{o} of \emph{fortis} cracked into \emph{ue}, the way it did in \emph{fuerza} and \emph{sueño}, so a Latin \emph{o} under stress became a Spanish \emph{ue} one more time.

English hoarded this family without merging any of it. A \textbf{fort} is a strong place, and so is a \textbf{fortress}. \textbf{Force} is \emph{fortia}, the same noun as \emph{fuerza}, arriving through French. An \textbf{effort} is strength pushed \emph{out}. To \textbf{fortify} is to make strong. \textbf{Fortitude} is strength held over time. And \textbf{comfort} is \emph{com-fortāre}, \emph{to strengthen thoroughly} — being comforted was once being made stronger, not being made softer.

\emph{Fuerte} ends in \emph{-e}, so it never switches: \emph{un café fuerte}, \emph{una chica fuerte}. And the second meaning is genuinely everyday — \emph{habla más fuerte} is \emph{speak louder}, not \emph{speak more strongly}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The adjective under \emph{la fuerza}, and a vowel break you can now predict.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{fuerte}
  \item \emph{la fuerza — fuerte}
  \item \emph{un café fuerte}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happened to the \emph{o} of \emph{fortis}? (Stressed, it broke into \emph{ue}.) And what did \emph{comfort} originally do to somebody? (Made them stronger.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[débil]{débil — the opposite of fuerte, and an accent that explains itself}

\label{lesson:ES-C327-debil}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{asleep}, then \emph{strong}. (\emph{Dormido}; \emph{fuerte}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{DÉ-bil}, the weight on the first beat. The \emph{b} is soft between vowels, and the \emph{l} stays bright rather than going dark at the end. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{débil} — \textquotedblleft{}weak.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{dēbilis} meant \emph{weak}, \emph{crippled}, \emph{without strength}. English took the long forms and left the short one: to \textbf{debilitate} is to weaken, a \textbf{debilitating} illness is one that takes your strength, and \textbf{debility} is the state of having none. English never adopted the plain adjective, so this is a word where Spanish keeps the simple version and English keeps only the dressed-up ones.

The written accent is not decoration and it is not random. Spanish has a default: a word ending in a vowel, in \emph{-n} or in \emph{-s} is stressed on the second-to-last beat, and any other ending pushes the stress onto the last beat. \emph{Débil} ends in \emph{-l}, so the default would make it \emph{de-BIL}. It is not \emph{de-BIL}; it is \emph{DÉ-bil}. The word breaks the rule, so it must carry an accent to say so. Every written accent in Spanish is that same announcement.

The ending never switches, because \emph{-l} is not \emph{-o}: \emph{un niño débil}, \emph{una niña débil}. And it pairs cleanly with the word before it — \emph{fuerte} and \emph{débil} are the two ends of one line.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The second pair, and the reason an accent mark appears where it does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{débil}
  \item \emph{fuerte — débil}
  \item \emph{estoy débil}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where would the stress fall without the accent? (On \emph{-bil}, because the word ends in \emph{-l}.) And which English verb is \emph{dēbilis} in a longer coat? (\emph{Debilitate}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sano]{sano — one Latin word that English split down the middle}

\label{lesson:ES-C327-sano}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{strong}, then \emph{weak}. (\emph{Fuerte}; \emph{débil}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item enfermo — the word this one answers.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SA-no}, two even beats, the weight on the first. The \emph{a} is open and short, and the \emph{n} is a clean tap with no nasal colour bleeding into the vowel. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sano} — \textquotedblleft{}healthy.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{sānus} covered the whole person: healthy in the body \emph{and} sound in the mind, with no line drawn between them. Spanish kept the word whole. English took it apart and put the halves in separate rooms.

The mind half went one way. \textbf{Sane} is \emph{sānus}, and so are \textbf{sanity} and \textbf{insane} — all of them now strictly about the mind, so that calling somebody \emph{sane} says nothing at all about their health. The body half went the other: \textbf{sanitary}, \textbf{sanitation} and a \textbf{sanatorium} are about physical health and never about the mind. One Latin word, and English speakers use both halves daily without hearing that they rhyme for a reason.

Spanish also kept the verb, \textbf{sanar}, \emph{to heal}, and a set phrase worth having: \textbf{sano y salvo} — \emph{safe and sound}, and both languages reached for a doubled expression to say the same thing.

The \emph{-o} switches: \textbf{sana}. And the pairing is the one you would expect — \emph{sano} answers \emph{enfermo}, the way \emph{fuerte} answers \emph{débil}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five reports from the body: awake, asleep, strong, weak, well. Between this chapter and the one before it you can now answer \emph{¿cómo estás?} ten ways.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sano}
  \item \emph{estoy sano}
  \item \emph{sano — enfermo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which half of \emph{sānus} did English keep in \emph{sane}? (The mind half.) And which half is in \emph{sanitary}? (The body half.)
\end{tcolorbox}
